=== Clarification of LSERO with Bilateral Contracting (5).pdf ===
Project No. 58777 Clarification of LSERO With Bilateral Contracting

Chairman and Commissioners:

Discussion during the April 1,2026 Senate Business and Commerce Committee meeting by
the senators, PUC Chairman, and ERCOT CEO has made it abundantly clear that a revised
market design is needed to get dispatchable generation built in Texas.

I submit this clarification to ensure that my proposal to modify the market design —LSERO
with Bilateral Contracting, filed in Project No. 58777—is not confused with the LSERO
construct evaluated in the 2021 E3/Garza study sponsored by NRG/EXELON. The old 4cp, %
of peak methodology with qualified resources has become obsolete.

LSERO with Bilateral Contracting is fundamentally different because it is built directly on
the Commission- approved Reliability Standard, which provides a proven and
transparent statistical method for determining how much dispatchable generation Texas
needs. Load Serving Entity Reliability Obligation (LSERO) is used in other reliability regions
but not in the same way as a Texas-style enhanced competitive model proposed here.
LSERO with Bilateral Contracting operates within the boundaries of the Texas energy-
only market but does not replace it.


1. The Reliability Standard Determines the Required
Dispatchable Capacity
The Commission has already adopted a probabilistic Reliability Standard for ERCOT. This
standard answers the central question—how much dispatchable generation is needed for
reliability—without relying on administrative planning constructs or top-down capacity
market models used in other regions. This approach is unique to Texas and is the most
directly focused, and simplest method for determining the reliability requirement.


2. Allocation of the Reliability Requirement to Each LSE
Once the total systemwide dispatchable requirement is determined, it is allocated to each
Load Serving Entity using firm load ratio share. This allocation requirement provides a
“level playing field” for competition that doesn’t exist in the present energy-only market.
Allocated dispatchable generation capacity is subject to ERCOT verification and firming
requirements for each LSE.
 3. Pricing Is Set Through Bilateral Contracting—Not
Through a Centralized Capacity Charge
This is the defining innovation of LSERO with Bilateral Contracting.

Under this proposal:

   •   There is no single statewide capacity price.
   •   There is no administratively determined charge.
   •   There is no centralized procurement.

Each LSE fulfills its Reliability Obligation through bilateral contracts already in use today!
Generation companies (Generators) compete to serve each LSE based on load shape,
customer mix, and resource strategy. Prices emerge from competition—not regulation.
Generators recover Cost of New Entry (CONE) through a competitive process at the local
level unique to every LSE.

This preserves and strengthens the Texas competitive model. The energy -only market
remains intact; only the Reliability Obligation within that market changes.


Why This Approach Works
Reliability replaces scarcity as the organizing principle. LSEs must first meet their
Reliability Obligation. Generators receive the steady revenue needed to finance and build
new dispatchable plants. The market no longer depends on rare price spikes to justify
investment.

Competition increases. Generators compete for every LSE’s reliability portfolio. LSEs
compete for customers using the best mix of resources. Renewables, batteries, and
demand side resources remain fully available. More competition means lower electric
rates for all Texans.

Texas retains its identity. This is not a capacity market, not an IRP, and not PCM. It is a
Texas-style Reliability Obligation supported by LSERO with Bilateral Contracting.
 Summary
The LSERO with Bilateral Contracting market design modification proposed in Project No.
58777

1. It should not be confused with the obsolete 2021 E3/Garza LSERO construct. 2. The
proposal enhances competition within the energy-only market but does not replace it. 3. It
introduces a “bottom-up” Texas-style competitive model unlike what is used in other
reliability regions. 4. It prioritizes reliability over scarcity. 5. Increased competition at
wholesale will lower costs to the ultimate consumer. 6. It provides the missing revenue
required by the generators through a competitive process, driving down the cost of CONE.
7.More competition means lower electric rates for all Texans.

LSERO with Bilateral Contracting is easy to understand and implement

Step 1: The Commission approved Reliability Standard determines how much
dispatchable generation is needed system wide. Step 2: The total dispatchable
requirement is allocated to each LSE using firm load ratio share. Step 3: Each LSE fulfills
its reliability obligation through bilateral contracts, preserving competition, and providing
generators with the stable revenue needed to build new plants.

Texas needs reliability to serve all the loads which will limit scarcity. LSERO with Bilateral
Contracting provides a competitive, financeable, and Texas appropriate path to get new
dispatchable generation built.

Respectfully submitted, Thomas L. Darte Greenville, Texas
